options.text: Building's longer axis is aligned North-South, causing maximum heat gain on broad facades
Alignment is diagonal, leading to significant solar heat gain during morning and afternoon.
Axis is partially oriented E-W, but significant broad wall areas still face direct E/W sun.
Major roof and wall axis is primarily East-West, significantly reducing heat gain
Optimized East-West alignment; minimal building depth on E/W facades to prevent solar heat soak.
Window openings are placed randomly or primarily on East/West walls with no solar strategy
Most openings are on E/W walls; North/South facades are underutilized for light/air
Equal distribution of windows across all facades; some attempt to favor N/S for light.
Primary openings are strategically located on North and South faces for controlled daylighting
Fully optimized N/S fenestration; 90%+ of windows are on N/S facades to maximize soft, consistent light.
Building is sealed or oriented to block prevailing winds; no natural ventilation potential
Some operable windows exist, but orientation does not align with local wind patterns
Building is oriented to catch some breeze, but internal layout obstructs cross-ventilation.
Openings are aligned with prevailing winds to scoop cool air in and exhaust warm air out
Optimized for passive cooling; aerodynamically oriented to maximize pressure differentials for 24/7 cross-ventilation
No external shading; large unshaded glass areas leading to high cooling loads
Basic internal blinds/curtains only; no structural shading of the building skin
Fixed overhangs exist on some windows but do not adequately block high-angle sun.
Comprehensive shading (fins, louvers, or deep overhangs) tailored specifically for N/S paths.
Dynamic or bio-climatic shading (e.g., automated louvers or dense greenery) fully protects all glazing
No insulation in walls/roof; high U-values leading to rapid heat transfer
Minimal insulation; some thermal bridging at junctions and structural members
Standard insulation (e.g., mineral wool) used; meets local baseline building codes.
High-performance materials (EPS-Expanded Polystyrene /AAC-Autoclaved Aerated Concrete) with thickness optimized for R-value; limited thermal bridging
Continuous high-performance insulation; zero thermal bridging design; U-values exceed NZEB standards
Fully glazed facade (>70% WWR); significant greenhouse effect and heat gain
High glazing ratio (50–70%); limited consideration for solar heat gain
Moderate glazing (40–50%); some effort to balance daylight and heat gain.
Optimized glazing ratio (30–40%); strategically placed to reduce cooling load
NZEB optimized ratio (<30% WWR on sun-facing facades); perfectly balanced for daylight and thermal control
Single-pane clear glass; no Low-E coatings; high Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC)
Double-pane glass but standard performance; basic shading to compensate for heat
Double-glazed with basic Low-E coating; meets standard energy efficiency ratings.
High-performance double/triple glazing with inert gas (Argon) and low SHGC (<0.25)
Super-insulated glazing; high visual light transmittance with extremely low U-values
Significant air leakage through cracks/junctions; no air barrier; drafty interior
Minor sealing efforts; no formal testing or measurement of infiltration rates
Standard construction sealing; complies with basic local airtightness requirements.
Integrated air barrier system; low leakage rates; verified by partial blower door testing
Passivhaus standard (ACH50 <= 0.6 h^-1); continuous air barrier from foundation to roof with MVHR integration
Aged systems (10+ years); Low Coefficient of Performance (COP)
Standard efficiency units; window or basic split ACs with no energy ratings
High-efficiency systems (e.g., Energy Star or 3-star rated); meets current energy codes.
Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) or VFD-enabled chillers; high part-load efficiency
NZEB optimized; ultra-high COP (>5.0); magnetic bearing chillers or advanced VRF with AI tuning.
ventilation relies on infiltration or simple exhaust fans
Basic mechanical ventilation with no energy recovery or filtration strategy
Controlled ventilation system; complies with ASHRAE 62.1 standards for air quality.
Dedicated Outdoor Air System (DOAS) with basic energy recovery wheels
Full Heat Recovery (HRV) or Enthalpy recovery; extracts energy from exhaust air to pre-cool incoming air
Single-zone control; All-on or All-off regardless of occupancy or solar gain
Basic multi-zone control with manual thermostats; limited precision
Thermostatic controls in major areas; some automatic scheduling.
Advanced zoning with Variable Air Volume (VAV) boxes and occupancy sensors
Granular, demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) using CO2 sensors and individual micro-zones
Reactive maintenance (repairs only upon system failure); no records
Periodic manual cleaning; basic logbooks but no performance tracking
Planned preventive maintenance; regular filter changes and refrigerant checks.
Condition-based monitoring; sensors alert staff to efficiency drops or leaks
Continuous Commissioning; digital twin or BMS-integrated diagnostics for peak efficiency
No available roof space or the roof is entirely shaded by nearby buildings/trees
Limited roof space; potential to cover <10% of the annual building EUI
Moderate roof space; potential to cover 10–30% of the annual building EUI.
Significant roof space; potential to cover 30–70% of the annual building EUI
Vast, unshaded roof space; potential to cover >70% of EUI on-site
No space for batteries; building electrical system is not compatible with renewables.
Basic electrical room; would require major retrofits to integrate solar or storage
Space exists for an inverter; building is wired for basic grid-tie solar.
Dedicated space for a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS); Solar Ready wiring in place
Storage Ready; Integrated BESS installed or space reserved with thermal management and smart grid controls
Only horizontal roof surfaces considered; no other renewable options
Potential for small-scale wind or solar on parking lots, but not yet assessed
Parking sheds or carports identified for Solar Canopy integration.
Building facade is suitable for Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) or solar fins
Multi-Surface Integration; Roof, Facades, and Carports all utilized for maximum energy harvest
Roof cannot support the weight of PV panels; no conduits for cabling
Structural capacity exists, but no infrastructure (conduits/access) for solar
Structural capacity verified; conduits for DC cabling are planned or partially installed.
Full structural and electrical capacity for a 100% EUI offset system
Structural mounts and electrical tie-ins are pre-installed for immediate scaling
Manual Controls Only: All systems (HVAC, Lighting) are turned on/off manually; no automation
Basic Thermostats: Stand-alone digital thermostats and timers are used for local control
Centralized BMS: A central system monitors and controls major building services from one interface
Sub-metering by Zone: BMS includes detailed energy sub-metering for specific floors, departments, or high-load equipment
AI-Driven / Demand Response: Fully automated AI that predicts energy needs and interacts with the grid for Demand Response
No energy data collected; only monthly utility bills are available
Manual monthly recording of main meter readings into a spreadsheet
Real-time monitoring of total building load with hourly data logging
15-minute interval data for all sub-meters; data is visualized in a dashboard.
High-Frequency Granularity: Real-time (second-by-second) data streaming with automated anomaly detection.
Systems operate in silos; HVAC, Lighting, and Fire systems do not communicate
Minimal integration; lighting and HVAC might share a basic schedule but no data
Major systems integrated via standard protocols (e.g., BACnet, Modbus) to a single BMS
Holistic Integration: All systems, including security and elevators, contribute data to energy optimization.
Full Interoperability: Plug-and-play integration with external IoT sensors and local renewable energy storage.
No automation; systems run 24/7 or rely on human memory to turn off
Simple time-clock scheduling (e.g., lights on at 8 AM, off at 6 PM)
Schedule-based automation with manual overrides for holidays or events
Occupancy-Based Control: Sensors automatically adjust HVAC/Lighting based on real-time room usage.
Predictive Control: System uses weather forecasts and occupancy trends to pre-cool or pre-heat spaces efficiently.
Reactive Repairs: Systems are only fixed after they break down; no regular upkeep
Basic Schedule: Filter changes and cleaning done once or twice a year, regardless of usage
Preventive Maintenance: Scheduled servicing based on manufacturer guidelines and run-hours
Data-Driven Maintenance: Uses BMS data and sensor alerts to service equipment before failure.
Continuous Commissioning: An ongoing process using real-time data to optimize energy and comfort 24/7.
Paper-based records or no records of equipment age, repair history, or efficiency
Basic spreadsheet (Excel) tracking of major assets and manual logbooks
CMMS Integration: Computerized Maintenance Management System used to track work orders
Digital Asset Tracking: QR codes/BIM used to access real-time repair history and energy data.
Digital Twin: A live virtual model of the building that simulates and optimizes maintenance needs.
No Commissioning: Systems have never been tested to see if they meet the original design intent
Initial Commissioning: Testing was done only during the building's original construction phase
Retro-Commissioning: Systems are re-tested and tuned every 3–5 years to fix performance drift.
Monitoring-Based Cx: Software tools continuously monitor system outputs for faults or energy waste.
Automated Continuous Cx: Automatically adjusts setpoints to maintain NZEB performance levels.
Sensors and thermostats are never calibrated; high risk of inaccurate readings
Calibration only occurs when a major system fails or comfort issues are reported
Periodic calibration of critical sensors (Temperature, CO2) every 2 years
Annual testing and calibration of all energy-impacting sensors and meters.
Self-Diagnostic Systems: Smart sensors that alert the team when they drift out of calibration.
No Energy Training: Staff are only trained in basic duties; no awareness of energy impact
General Facilities Staff: Standard FM training focused on keeping things running rather than efficiency
Green Building Trained: Staff hold basic certifications or have attended workshops on LEED/GreenSL principles
Certified Energy Manager (CEM): A formally certified professional oversees energy audits and efficiency planning.
NZEB Specialist On-Site: Dedicated expert with specific NZEB operational certification and deep systems-thinking skills.
Staff cannot operate the BMS; rely entirely on external vendors for any system changes
Can view basic BMS dashboards but cannot adjust setpoints or diagnose alarms
Proficient in standard BMS operations, scheduling, and basic troubleshooting.
Advanced use of analytics software to identify energy waste in real-time.
Expert Digital Fluency: Able to reprogram control logic and integrate new IoT sensors or AI tools independently.
No performance targets; staff are not incentivized or evaluated based on energy savings
Unofficial interest in saving energy, but no formal recognition or goals
Energy savings are a part of the annual facility performance review
KPI-Driven Team: Clear monthly energy reduction targets with financial or career incentives for the team.
Culture of Excellence: Total team alignment; energy conservation is a core value in every operational decision.
Knowledge is in the head of one person; no documentation or training for new hires
Informal on-the-job shadowing; no structured energy training materials
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for energy management are documented
Digital knowledge base exists with video tutorials and training logs for all technical staff.
Continuous Learning Hub: Structured, ongoing training program that evolves with new technologies.
No Engagement: Occupants are unaware of the building’s energy goals or their impact on them
Signage/Posters: Basic Turn off lights stickers or general sustainability posters are visible
Monthly Energy Reports: Periodic newsletters or reports are shared with occupants regarding usage
Tenant Dashboards: Real-time digital displays in lobbies or apps showing live energy consumption data.
Direct Energy-Use Incentives: Financial rewards, rent credits, or Green Leases that reward tenants for hitting NZEB targets.
No individual control; occupants often use personal fans to stay comfortable
Limited manual control (local switches) but often left on after hours
Occupants can adjust local settings within a Green Range (e.g., +/- 2 degrees)
Adaptive comfort settings; occupants are prompted to use natural ventilation when appropriate.
Biophilic & Smart Control: Occupants use a personal app to vote on comfort levels, which the AI uses to optimize the whole floor.
No policy; personal electronics (kettles, chargers) are used and left plugged in 24/7
Informal requests to unplug; cleaning staff may turn off some items
Formal After-Hours policy; designated Power-Down zones for shared equipment
Smart power strips and Master Switches used to kill standby power automatically.
Total Plug-Load Integration: All personal equipment is energy-rated and integrated into the building’s energy budget.
No orientation for new tenants/employees regarding the building's Green features
Basic welcome flyer mentioning recycling and light switches
Annual Sustainability Day or workshop to explain building features and EUI targets
Continuous feedback loops; occupants receive prompts when their behaviour deviates from NZEB goals.
Active Participants: Occupants are trained as Energy Champions and actively participate in annual NZEB audits.
No Budget Available: There is no capital allocated for energy efficiency; any spending is for emergency repairs only
Case-by-Case Approval: Energy projects must be proposed individually and compete with all other business expenses for funding
Annual Green Budget: A recurring yearly budget is set aside specifically for sustainability and energy-saving projects
Multi-Year Retrofit Fund: A long-term sinking fund or ring-fenced capital exists to support phased deep energy retrofits.
Dedicated Net-Zero Capital: Specific, high-volume capital is secured and ready for full NZEB transition (e.g., Solar PV + Full HVAC overhaul).
Financial decisions are made solely on the lowest initial purchase price (First Cost)
Energy efficiency is considered only if the equipment is already being replaced
Life-Cycle Cost is considered, but short-term ROI still dictates most investment decisions
Projects are prioritized based on their contribution to the building's NZEB roadmap, not just immediate ROI.
Carbon-Weighted Investing: Capital is allocated based on the Cost of Carbon Avoided alongside financial returns.
Energy savings from efficiency projects go back into the general profit pool with no tracking
Savings are tracked but are used to reduce overall operating expenses (OpEx) without being reinvested
A portion of energy savings is informally recognized as proof to justify future small projects
Internal Carbon Fee: The building charges itself for energy waste, using that money to fund further green upgrades.
Self-Funding Model (Revolving Fund): 100% of verified energy savings are automatically reinvested into the next NZEB project.
No Green procurement policy; vendors are selected based on the lowest bid only
Vendors are asked about their environmental policy, but it carries no weight in the final selection
Minimum efficiency standards are included in all procurement contracts for new equipment
Vendors must provide verified energy ratings or performance guarantees for all major assets.
Performance-Based Contracting: Vendors are paid based on the actual energy savings their equipment or service achieves..(marks =
<1 Year Required: Only projects with near-instant payback are considered
2-4 Year Requirement: Standard commercial horizon; limits investment to like LEDs
5-7 Year Requirement: Typical Green Building horizon; allows for basic HVAC and sensor upgrades
8-10 Year Requirement: Long-term strategic horizon; allows for significant renewable energy and envelope upgrades
Lifecycle Cost (LCC) Approach: Decisions are based on total cost of ownership over 10+ years, accounting for rising energy costs
Energy efficiency is not factored into the building's market value or rental rates
General awareness that green is better, but no formal impact on asset valuation
Building marketed as Efficient; basic premium on rental or resale value due to low OpEx
Formal valuation includes energy savings and carbon risk mitigation as a core asset value
NZEB Asset Premium: Building is valued as a future-proof asset; zero carbon risk leads to lower insurance/finance rates
No consideration for future electricity price hikes or carbon taxes
Reactive approach to utility price changes; no long-term energy risk planning
Periodic analysis of energy market trends; basic budget buffers for price volatility
Active energy risk management; hedging and efficiency used to protect against utility spikes
Resilience-Based Finance: Investment is prioritized specifically to eliminate energy price risk and carbon tax liability.
Unaware of Options: No knowledge of specialized green loans, grants, or tax incentives available for retrofits
Aware but No Action: General knowledge exists, but no formal inquiries or applications have been initiated
Applied for Green Loans: Currently in the process of applying for or has previously used basic sustainability grants
Secured Green Financing: Utilizing low-interest Green Loans specifically for deep energy upgrades
Utilizing Carbon Offsets/PPAs: Leveraging advanced tools like Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) or selling Carbon Credits to fund the NZEB transition
No utilization of government or utility-based rebates; all upgrades are 100% self-funded
Ad-hoc use of small rebates (e.g., lighting equipment rebates) when convenient
Systemic tracking and application for all available local and national energy efficiency incentives
Strategic alignment with utility Demand Response programs to generate recurring revenue
Maximum Subsidy Optimization: Every available tax credit, grant, and utility incentive is integrated into the project's financial stack
Traditional Bid-and-Build contracts with no guarantees on actual energy savings
Standard maintenance contracts with basic service level agreements (SLAs)
Service contracts include minor clauses regarding energy efficiency performance
Energy Performance Contracting (EPC): Using a third party Energy Service Company (ESCO) to fund and guarantee energy savings over time
Energy-as-a-Service: Paying for comfort or lighting as a service, where the provider owns the risk and the energy bill.
No Asset Link: Building value is based purely on location and square footage; energy performance is ignored in appraisals
Basic Awareness: General understanding that efficiency reduces OpEx, but no formal data is used during valuation
Marketing as Green: Building is marketed using its green certifications (e.g., LEED/Green Mark) to attract high-quality tenants
Premium Green Rental Rate: Tangible evidence that the building commands higher rent or lower vacancy rates due to its efficiency
Net-Zero Asset Valuation: The building is valued as a Future-Proof asset; Net-Zero status is a core multiplier in the final appraisal
Energy costs are viewed as a fixed cost that cannot be changed; no impact on Net Operating Income (NOI)
OpEx is tracked, but savings from efficiency are not explicitly linked to increased property value
Efficiency projects are justified by their direct impact on increasing Net Operating Income (NOI)
Real-time energy data is used to provide transparent Total Occupancy Cost estimates to prospective tenants
OpEx Minimization: Energy costs are so low/predictable that the building has a significant competitive advantage in the market
No awareness of Stranded Asset risk; no concern that the building might become obsolete due to climate laws
Awareness that future regulations might require upgrades, but no financial risk is modeled
Basic risk assessment of potential Carbon Taxes or fines for poor building performance
Financial modeling includes the Value at Risk (VaR) from upcoming environmental mandates or local laws
Resilience Premium: Resilience to carbon taxes and grid instability secures the property’s value as a low-risk asset
No ESG Policy: No environmental or social governance policy exists; sustainability is not a corporate priority
Generic Sustainability Goal: A public statement exists (e.g., We aim to be green), but lacks specific metrics or deadlines
Net-Zero Target Set: A formal commitment to achieve Net-Zero by a specific date (e.g., 2040) is signed by leadership
Detailed NZEB Roadmap: A step-by-step technical and financial plan is in place to reach the Net-Zero goal for this specific building
Verified Science-Based Target: Goals are externally verified and aligned with the 1.5 Celcius Paris Agreement pathway
No executive oversight; sustainability tasks are assigned to junior staff with no budget authority
A Green Committee exists but has no formal power to influence major CAPEX decisions
A Sustainability Manager or Director reports to the board on energy performance annually
Energy and Carbon targets are part of the CEO/Executive performance and compensation package
Board-Level Accountability: The Board of Directors actively reviews NZEB progress quarterly as a core business risk/opportunity
No internal cost assigned to carbon emissions or energy waste
General awareness of carbon footprint, but it does not affect internal project approvals
Shadow carbon pricing is used to test how future taxes might impact the building's bottom line
An actual internal carbon fee is charged to departments/tenants based on their energy use
Carbon-Positive Reinvestment: Revenue from internal carbon fees is 100% dedicated to funding NZEB retrofits
No Energy Disclosure: Energy data is considered private; no internal or external sharing of performance
Internal Tracking Only: Energy data is recorded for accounting purposes but is not shared outside the finance/FM team
Annual Green Reporting: Building performance is summarized in a yearly Sustainability or ESG report for stakeholders

Public Carbon Disclosure: Detailed carbon footprint (Scope 1-Direct Emissions & 2-Indirect Emissions) is published on platforms like CDP (Carbon Disclosure Project) or GRESB (Global Real Estate Sustainability Benchmark)
Real-Time Public Dashboard: Live energy and carbon intensity data are displayed on a public website or lobby screen
No comparison with similar buildings; no awareness of how the building performs against its peers
Informal comparison with previous years' bills; no external benchmarking used
Standard Benchmarking: Building is ranked against national averages
Active Peer Competition: Building participates in regional Green Building challenges or leaderboards
Market Leader Status: The building sets the regional benchmark for NZEB performance, influencing local policy and standards
No external audits; energy data is self-reported and never verified for accuracy
Periodic internal reviews of energy bills, but no formal technical audit process
Annual Energy Audit: A professional third-party auditor reviews the building’s energy systems and data once a year
Third-Party Data Verification: Carbon and energy data are verified by an accredited body (e.g., ISO 14064 or equivalent)
Continuous Digital Audit: BMS data is automatically verified in real-time by a third-party digital platform to ensure NZEB integrity.
No Grid Interaction: Building is either off-grid or has a passive, one-way connection with no ability to manage flow
Standard Connection: Simple utility connection; building consumes power as needed without any intelligence or feedback
Net-Metering Enabled: The building is legally and technically equipped to export excess solar power back to the grid
Smart-Grid Ready: Building can respond to grid signals (Price-based or Load-based) to shift its energy demand
Virtual Power Plant (VPP): The building acts as a grid resource, aggregating solar and battery storage to support grid stability
No capability to reduce load during grid peaks; high Peak Demand charges
Manual load shedding (turning off non-essential lights) during power shortages or peak hours
Automated Load Shedding: BMS automatically dims lights or adjusts AC setpoints when notified of a grid peak
Active Demand Response: Building participates in utility programs, receiving payments to reduce load on demand
Bi-Directional Support: Building uses on-site batteries to feed the grid during shortages
Building fails to meet current minimum national energy efficiency or building codes
Compliant with basic building codes but makes no effort to exceed them
Exceeds Local Code: Building is designed to Green Building standards that go beyond the legal minimum
Pre-Compliant for NZEB: Already meets future mandated efficiency codes that are not yet legally required.
Policy Trailblazer: Building performance is so high it is used by regulators to draft new NZEB national standards
Below Current Code: Building fails to meet current minimum national energy efficiency or building codes
Meets Baseline Code: Compliant with basic building codes but makes no effort to exceed the legal minimum requirements
Exceeds Green Building Code: Building performance surpasses standard green certifications (e.g., LEED Silver/Gold or SLGBC)
Prepared for Future Mandates: Already meets proposed future energy codes (e.g., 2030 targets) before they are legally enforced
Defines Local Best Practice: The building’s performance is so high it is used as a case study for drafting new national NZEB standards
No process for checking code compliance; building has not been audited since original construction
Informal internal checks for compliance, usually only during major renovations
Regular internal audits to ensure the building stays compliant with evolving local environmental laws
Automated compliance tracking via digital tools that alert management to new or upcoming regulations
Proactive Compliance: Building is continuously updated to stay ahead of the most stringent international NZEB standards
No voluntary green certifications; building is viewed strictly as a standard asset
Currently exploring certification options but has not yet registered for any program
Holds an active baseline green certification (e.g., LEED Certified, Green Mark, or SLGBC rating)
Holds a high-level Gold or Platinum rating in a recognized green building system
NZEB/Net-Zero Certified: Holds a verified Net-Zero Energy certification from an accredited body
No awareness of potential fines or legal penalties for energy waste or high carbon emissions
Aware of potential penalties but has no financial or operational plan to mitigate these risks
Basic legal strategy in place to ensure compliance with current local and national environmental mandates
Comprehensive risk mitigation plan including upgrades scheduled to avoid future carbon tax liabilities
Zero Legal Risk: Building exceeds all possible regulatory requirements; it is legally future-proofed against any climate policy
